sentences.text: The type specimen of Kaatedocus consists of a well-preserved skull and cervical vertebrae found in the lower Morrison Formation.
The type individual was estimated to be approximately 14 meters long, indicating a body weight of 14 tonnes.
The skull is flattened and wide, featuring narrow teeth at the front as deduced from tooth cavities since the teeth themselves are lost.
The tail vertebrae possess a single keel.
Tschopp suggests that larger adult specimens could have reached a length of 16 to 18 meters.
At roughly 14 meters long and weighing 14 tonnes, this animal was relatively small compared to most diplodocids.
Kaatedocus siberi was named in 2012 by Emanuel Tschopp and Octávio Mateus.
The genus name combines a reference to its relative Diplodocus with the diminutive suffix ~kaate from the Crow language, while the species name honors Hans-Jakob Siber.
A specimen previously thought to be Barosaurus was reinterpreted as Kaatedocus in 2015 based on phylogenetic analysis.
Only 10% of the originally discovered fossils survived, including a skull, but the site was reopened in 1989 by Hans-Jakob Siber, who found an additional 450 bones at the adjacent Cantera Quarry.
Research by Andreas Christian and Armin Schmitt suggests that Kaatedocus held its neck in a vertical position, confirmed by studies of its vestibular system.
Kaatedocus is a member of the class Saurischia.
It is classified within the family Diplodocidae and the subfamily Diplodocinae.
However, it also belongs to the parent group Dicraeosauridae and is classified in the family Dicraeosauridae.
Whitlock and Wilson (2020) argue that Kaatedocus is the most basal dicraeosaurid, a position they consider more likely than being a diplodocid.
In 2017, Tschopp and Mateus positioned Kaatedocus as the most basal diplodocine during a phylogenetic review associated with the description of the genus Galeamopus.
Kaatedocus lived during the Middle Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian stage) in what is now northern Wyoming, United States, between 154.8 and 149.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether certain skull features of Kaatedocus are specific to Diplodocidae or general traits of Flagellicaudata, as it is unknown if dicraeosaurids possessed these features.
